analysis.one_liner: Requires FTC rules forcing websites to disclose and limit how they collect, use, and sell people's personal information.
analysis.headline: The bill was never voted on: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from October 2000 until that Congress ended in January 2001, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules for websites and online services handling personal information such as names, addresses, email, and Social Security numbers. Sites would have to post clear notices about what they collect and who they sell it to, give visitors a simple way to opt out of having data shared for unrelated purposes, and stop matching IP addresses to personal information without a prior business relationship. Enforcement would come through the FTC, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits with damages up to $50,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet users age 13 and older, who would gain notice of what data is collected about them, a way to opt out of data sharing, and legal remedies if sites misuse their information.

how_it_helps.text: Websites and online services would have to post clear notices identifying the operator, what personal information is collected, how it is used, and what may be sold or shared with other companies.
Operators would have to provide a simple online process letting individuals opt out of the disclosure of personal information for purposes unrelated to why it was collected.
Websites and internet service providers would be barred from correlating IP address information with personal information unless a pre-existing business relationship exists.

Individuals could sue for actual monetary loss or at least $1,000 per violation (capped at $50,000), with treble damages for willful violations, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of residents.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial website operators, online services, internet service providers, and the data-driven advertising businesses that profit from collecting and reselling personal information, which would face compliance costs, limits on data use, and lawsuit exposure.

drawbacks.text: The private right of action with a $1,000 statutory minimum per violation, plus state attorney general suits, could expose even small commercial websites to costly litigation over technical compliance rather than actual harm.

The bill covers any commercial website collecting personal information in interstate commerce, so small businesses and startups would bear notice, opt-out, and recordkeeping burdens alongside large data brokers.

The opt-out standard is weaker than an opt-in: data could be shared unless the individual affirmatively objects, and the purpose limit does not apply to transactional information or data used for the operator's own business activities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real but modest: notice and opt-out rather than a ban on data collection, with broad carve-outs for the operator's own uses. The main cost falls on website operators and the data brokerage and online advertising industries, in compliance spending and litigation exposure under a private right of action that some would call overbroad. On balance the bill asked an industry built on unpaid-for personal data to bear real costs in exchange for consumer control, and it died before any of those tradeoffs were debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2000 and referred to the House Commerce Committee and its Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection Subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2001 — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Gene Green introduced the Consumer Online Privacy and Disclosure Act on October 10, 2000.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day, and on October 25 to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection.
No further action was taken; the bill had no cosponsors and died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Website operators, online advertising and data brokerage businesses, and other companies whose models depend on collecting and selling personal information, which avoided federal privacy rules for another two decades.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that profit from personal data

for.name: Rep. Gene Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on October 25, 2000.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 25, 2000 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition ever formed in the record.

industries.note: These businesses profit by collecting, correlating, and reselling personal information, including the IP-address-to-person matching the bill would bar without a prior business relationship. The bill would have cut directly into that revenue, and its failure left the industry's data practices unregulated at the federal level.

Operators would face notice, opt-out, and compliance requirements and potential liability, but sites whose value depends on unrestricted data collection would bear the largest burden. Small operators and startups would bear the same compliance costs as large ones.
